title: The Scroll and the Slain Lamb
summary: The One on the throne holds a scroll sealed with seven seals, and no one in all creation is worthy to open it, so John weeps. An elder tells him the Lion of Judah has triumphed, but when John looks he sees a Lamb that has been slain, standing at the center of the throne. The Lamb takes the scroll, and heaven and then all creation break into songs of worship to God and to the Lamb together.
story: Chapter 4 showed the throne room and the worship of God the creator. Chapter 5 adds the drama that drives the rest of the book: a sealed scroll in God's right hand, and the question of who can open it. The scroll holds God's purposes for the world, his judgment and his redemption, and until it is opened those purposes are not carried out. The answer is the crucified and risen Jesus, pictured as a Lamb bearing the marks of slaughter yet standing alive. From here the Lamb breaks the seals one by one (chapter 6), and every judgment and deliverance in the chapters that follow comes from his hand. This is the hinge of Revelation: history is opened by the one who was slain.
historical:
The scene is heavenly, but its first hearers lived in cities full of imperial ceremony. Emperors entered cities to acclamations, their images were honored with hymns and incense, and Nero kept a trained corps of young men to lead the applause when he performed, as both Suetonius and Tacitus report. Scholars have long noted how the hymns of Revelation 4 and 5 resemble the language of such acclamations, while redirecting it: the one truly worthy of power and riches and glory is not the emperor but the Lamb who was killed by imperial power.

The detail of seven seals may also have been familiar. Roman wills were commonly sealed by seven witnesses and opened only at the proper time by the proper person, and some interpreters think John's hearers would have heard the scroll as a testament whose inheritance could be released only by the rightful heir. Others see instead the sealed book of Daniel 12:4, closed until the time of the end, or the scroll written on front and back in Ezekiel 2:9-10.
cultural:
The titles in verse 5 are Israel's messianic hopes. The Lion of Judah recalls Jacob's blessing of Judah as a lion from whom the scepter would not depart (Genesis 49:9-10). The Root of David recalls Isaiah 11, the shoot from Jesse's stump on whom the Spirit rests. Jewish readers expected a conquering king. John hears of a lion and then sees a Lamb, and the Greek word is a small, even tender one. The lamb recalls the Passover lambs whose blood marked Israel's doors in Egypt (Exodus 12) and the servant of Isaiah 53, led like a lamb to slaughter. The seven horns picture complete power (horns are a standard biblical image of strength, as in Daniel 7), and the seven eyes come from Zechariah 4:10, the eyes of the LORD that range through all the earth.

The harps and golden bowls of incense belong to temple worship. The Psalms picture prayer rising like incense (Psalm 141:2), and John says so directly: the incense is the prayers of the saints (a New Testament word for all God's holy people, not a special class). The new song is a phrase from the Psalms and Isaiah for praise at a fresh act of salvation. The redeemed are made a kingdom and priests, the calling God gave Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:6), now extended to people from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation. The countless angels echo Daniel 7:10.
literary: Revelation often works by hearing and then seeing. John hears “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” and sees “a Lamb who appeared to have been slain”, and the second reinterprets the first: the messianic victory is won by sacrificial death. The same pattern returns in chapter 7, where he hears the number 144,000 and sees a multitude no one can count. The chapter builds in widening circles of worship: first the living creatures and elders (vv. 8-10), then myriads of angels (vv. 11-12), then every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea (v. 13), and finally a closing “Amen”. The hymns also grow, from a song with a reason attached (“because You were slain”) to a sevenfold acclamation of power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing. The last hymn is addressed jointly: “To Him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb”.

outline.t: A sealed scroll, and no one worthy to open it
The Lion who is a Lamb takes the scroll
The new song of the creatures and elders
Myriads of angels acclaim the Lamb
All creation worships God and the Lamb

doctrines.note: The Lamb is worthy “because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.” His death is a costly purchase, a ransom that brings people to God, and it is the ground of his authority over history.
Jesus fulfills Israel's hope for a king from Judah and the root of David, but he conquers by dying. The chapter redefines messianic power as self-giving sacrifice.

The One on the throne and the Lamb receive the same worship, and the seven Spirits are the Lamb's eyes sent into all the earth. The church read passages like this as witness to one God known as Father, Son, and Spirit.
The redeemed are drawn from every nation and made a kingdom and priests. The people of God is multi-ethnic by design, and its calling is to serve God and reign with him.

words.note: Arnion, lamb. Grammatically a diminutive, it is Revelation's main title for Christ, used of him twenty-eight times in the book (and once, in parody, of the second beast in 13:11). It joins vulnerability to authority: the Lamb has seven horns and takes the scroll from God's right hand. Elsewhere in the New Testament it appears only in John 21:15, of Jesus' flock.

Sphazō, to slaughter, used of sacrificial killing and of violent death. The Lamb stands “as slain”, alive yet still bearing the marks, and the same word describes the martyrs in 6:9. Revelation deliberately parodies it in 13:3, where a head of the beast only appears to have been mortally wounded.

Agorazō, to buy in the marketplace. The picture is of a purchase that transfers ownership, as with a slave bought out of one household into another. People from every nation now belong to God because the Lamb paid for them with his blood.
Biblion, a scroll or document. In the ancient world a biblion could be a book, a legal deed, or a will. Its seven seals mean it is fully closed; only one with the right authority may open it.

christ: Revelation 5 is one of the highest moments of Christology (teaching about who Christ is) in the New Testament. The Lamb shares the throne, standing at its center; he takes the scroll from God's own hand; and he receives the worship that chapter 4 gave to God alone, from the whole creation, in a single joint doxology. Yet Revelation is fiercely monotheistic: when John later falls at an angel's feet he is told to worship God only (19:10; 22:8-9). The only way to hold both is the church's confession that the Son is truly God, one with the Father, and not a second deity. The chapter also shows what he has done. He conquered by being slain, bought a people with his blood, and made them a royal priesthood. The marks of the cross are not erased by the resurrection; the risen Christ reigns as the slain Lamb, and that is how God's purposes for the world are opened.

hard.q: If only God is to be worshiped, how can the Lamb be worshiped alongside him without making two gods?
hard.a:
The question is a fair one, and Revelation raises it itself. Jewish faith in the first century prayed to one God and refused worship to any creature, and Revelation shares that conviction completely: John is twice rebuked for kneeling to an angel. A thoughtful reader might suspect the book of contradicting itself or of quietly adding a second god.

The church's answer, worked out over the first four centuries and confessed in the Nicene Creed (AD 325, expanded in 381), is that the worship of the Lamb is not the worship of a second being alongside God but the worship of the one God, who is Father, Son, and Spirit. Scholars of early Christianity have noted how quickly this pattern of devotion to Jesus appeared among Jewish believers, well before the creeds gave it technical language. Revelation 5 does not explain the Trinity, but it shows the worship that the doctrine of the Trinity was formulated to account for: the Lamb is included in the identity of the one God without God ceasing to be one.

questions: John expected a lion and saw a slain lamb. Where do you expect God to act with force when he may be working through faithfulness and suffering instead?
The redeemed come from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation. How well does your own church reflect that, and what would it take to reflect it more?
The prayers of the saints are kept in golden bowls before the throne. How does it change your prayers to know that none of them are lost?
